Time : about 45 minutes. Runs : the small scripts below run here; nothing needs an API key. In plain words first The idea in one line A forward deployed engineer sits with a customer, writes the code that puts a model into their real work, and stays until the people doing that work rely on it. The problem A model that scores well in a demo is not yet a deployment. Between the demo and value sit the customer's messy data, their access rules, their security team, the people whose jobs change, and a long tail of edge cases nobody wrote down. Product teams cannot see that tail from headquarters, and advisers who only recommend cannot close it. The forward deployed engineer exists to close it: an engineer who is measured on whether the customer's outcome actually moves, not on whether a feature shipped. The term comes from Palantir, which sent engineers to work on site with government and enterprise customers in the 2000s. AI labs revived it because deploying language models has the same shape: the model is general, the value is specific, and the specific part is engineering work inside someone else's systems. In October 2026 Anthropic launched Claude Frontier Academy, with a $100 million commitment to train 10,000 such engineers by the end of 2027. What the job is, and what it is not Role Writes production code in the customer's environment Owns the business outcome Typical horizon Forward deployed engineer Yes, daily Yes Weeks to months per use case, often longer per customer Solutions engineer or architect Rarely; demos and reference designs Shares it with sales Pre-sale to launch Consultant Sometimes, usually advisory Recommends; the customer owns it Fixed engagement Product engineer In the vendor's own product Owns product metrics, not one customer's Ongoing ML engineer Models and pipelines Owns model quality Ongoing Three things set the FDE apart. First, they build inside the customer's environment , with the customer's identity system, data and tooling, not against anonymised samples. Second, they own the outcome : OpenAI's FDE teams describe success as a system in production that keeps its eval scores; Palantir talks about impact on the customer's goal; Ramp ties FDE work to customer outcomes and revenue. Third, they feed the field back into the product : what one customer needed often becomes a feature for every customer. The shape of an engagement Every lesson in this phase is a stage of one engagement. The running case throughout is Harbor Mutual , a fictional mid-sized insurer whose claims team spends hours turning emails, PDFs and photos into claim records. You will produce one artefact per stage, and together they form a deployment dossier. Stage Question it answers Artefact you produce Lessons Discover Who needs what, and who decides? Time : about 50 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line An engagement is a series of gates; each gate has a question, an artefact that answers it, and a person who signs it off. The problem Engagements rarely fail at the model. They fail because a stage was skipped: nobody measured today's baseline, so the pilot cannot prove anything; security saw the design in week ten instead of week two; the people who do the work were never asked. A lifecycle with explicit gates makes those skips visible while they are still cheap to fix. The stages and their exit tests Stage Exit test (you may move on when...) Signed off by Discover You can state the problem in the customer's words, with a number attached Business sponsor Qualify The use case scores above your bar on value, feasibility, data, risk and adoption Sponsor and your own lead Map and scope The workflow is mapped from observation, and acceptance criteria are written as evals Sponsor and process owner Prototype A thin slice runs end to end on real (or realistic) data with traces You, then the process owner Trust Security review passed, eval suite green, cost per transaction known Security, data owner Pilot A named group used it for a fixed period; results compared with the baseline Sponsor Production and adoption Usage is steady without you pushing it; incidents have an owner Process owner, IT operations Handover The customer's team runs, changes and switches it off without you System owner Two stages are often merged by accident and should not be: prototype answers "can it work?", pilot answers "does it work here, for these people?". A prototype can use synthetic data and one enthusiastic user; a pilot cannot. Plan backwards from the handover Customers ask "when will it be live?". The honest answer is a plan that starts at the handover date and works back, with buffers where uncertainty is highest. The script lays out a 12-week plan for Harbor Mutual and shows which gates sit on the critical path. Copy What you should see Copy Copy "Trust" runs alongside the prototype on purpose: security review takes calendar time, not effort, so it should start the week the design exists. Where engagements stall Watch out Four common stalls No baseline. Nobody measured the current cycle time or error rate, so the pilot readout is opinion against opinion. Measure in discovery, before anything changes. Late security. The security team sees the design after it is built and asks for changes that unwind it. Show them the trust boundary in week two. Pilot without users. The pilot group is the project team. Pick people who do the work daily and have no stake in the project's success. Hidden owner. Nobody on the customer side owns the system after launch, so the FDE never leaves. Name the owner at scoping time and make them sign the handover. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A pilot needs real users doing real work for a fixed period; a prototype does not. ✗ Security review should come after the pilot, once the design is final. It takes calendar time and can force design changes, so it starts as soon as the design exists. ✓ Each stage has an exit test and a named person who signs it off. Recap What to keep Stages are gates: question, artefact, signer. Plan back from the handover date; run security in parallel with building. Measure the baseline before anything changes. Exercises Change the plan so the pilot is four weeks and the handover date cannot move. Which stage absorbs the week, and is that safe? For each stage, write the one-sentence exit test for Harbor Mutual specifically (for example, "Qualify: fit score at least 3.5 of 5 and an ROI over 12 months"). List who at a typical insurer would sign each gate. Which person is most likely to be missing from the first meeting? Time : about an hour. In plain words first The idea in one line Four decisions set the ceiling on quality before you write a prompt: where people meet Claude, which model, which features, and what goes into its context. The problem Teams often start with "let's call the API" and later discover the users live in Slack, the data sits behind a connector that already exists, or a chat product with a shared project would have solved half the problem on day one. Choosing the entry point first, then the model, then features, then context, saves rebuilding. Decision 1: the entry point Entry point Who uses it Good for You build Claude apps and Claude Enterprise (projects, connectors, skills) Knowledge workers Assisted work where a person stays in the loop; fastest time to value Configuration, connectors, skills, training Claude Code Engineers, and automation in CI Software work in repositories; scripted, verified changes Repository memory, permissions, hooks, skills Claude API (Developer Platform) Your application A step inside an existing system or product; full control of prompts, tools, data The application around the model Claude Agent SDK Your application Long-running agents with Claude Code's harness: tools, permissions, subagents, sessions The agent's tools, policies and host A useful rule: start at the highest-level entry point that meets the requirement , and move down only when you need control it cannot give. A claims handler drafting replies may be fully served by a shared project with the right connectors; automatic intake of 3,000 emails a day into a claims system needs the API or the Agent SDK. Decision 2: the model and effort Current models, from the Claude documentation (November 2026): Claude Haiku 5.5 is the fastest and cheapest, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is fast with strong quality, Claude Opus 5.5 is built for long-running agentic and knowledge work, and Claude Fable 5.2 is the most capable and most expensive. All four have a 1M-token context window and up to 128K output tokens. Thinking is adaptive; you steer depth with the effort parameter rather than a token budget. The habit to build: pick by measured quality on your eval set, then by cost and latency , not by brand. Route easy, high-volume steps (classifying an email) to a small model and keep the strongest model for the steps where errors are expensive. Decision 3: the features Copy What you should see Copy Copy Overnight claim intake needs almost every feature, and batch pricing halves its model cost because no one is waiting for the answer. Decision 4: the context What the model sees decides most of what it can do. For each request, list what goes in: instructions, the customer's policies, the documents for this case, tool results, examples of good output. Then ask what must never go in (another customer's data, secrets, fields the user may not see). Lesson 31.10 covers retrieval and permissions in detail. Choose by measured quality on your evals, then cost and latency; route easy, high-volume steps to smaller models. ✓ Work that does not need an answer immediately is a candidate for the Batches API. Recap What to keep Entry point, model, features, context: decide them in that order. Pick models by your eval results, then price and speed. Time : about an hour. In plain words first The idea in one line Find out who pays, who uses, who owns and who can say no, then watch the work before you believe the description of it. The problem The person who asks for an AI project is rarely the person who does the work, and neither of them is the person who can block it. Harbor Mutual's claims director wants "faster claims"; the handlers want fewer copy-paste steps; IT wants nothing new to support; security wants no customer data leaving approved systems. A plan that satisfies only the director will stall at the other three. The stakeholder map Role At Harbor Mutual What they need to say yes Typical question Sponsor (pays, sets the goal) Claims director A number that moves (cycle time, cost per claim) "What will it save?" Users (do the work) Claims handlers Less tedious work, no new risk to them "Will this make my day harder?" Process owner (owns the system after launch) Claims operations lead Something they can run and change "Who fixes it at 2 a.m.?" Gatekeepers Security, privacy, legal, IT Evidence the risks are controlled "Where does the data go?" Your side Account team, product A repeatable win "Can we reuse this?" Discovery is complete when each row has a name, and you know what each person needs to say yes. Questions that open the problem Ask about the work, not the AI: Walk me through the last claim you processed. What did you open first? What did you copy where? What took longest? What went wrong last week? How do you know a claim is done? What does a mistake cost? Then ask for the number: how many a day, how long each, how many come back for rework? Then shadow . FDE teams put it as "become users before you become builders": an hour beside a handler shows steps no one mentions in meetings, such as asking a colleague in chat who owns a policy, or re-keying a date because two systems use different formats. From notes to ranked pain points After five or six conversations you have pages of notes. Tagging each pain with who said it, and counting distinct people rather than mentions, keeps one loud voice from setting the agenda. Copy What you should see Copy Copy "Chasing missing documents" has three independent voices and the largest time cost: that, not the director's general wish, is the first problem to scope. The problem statement End discovery with one paragraph the sponsor agrees to in writing: Claims handlers spend about 10 minutes per claim chasing missing documents and 5 re-keying policy data, across roughly 400 claims a day. We will reduce handler time per claim by at least 8 minutes without raising the error rate, measured over a four-week pilot against a two-week baseline. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Counting distinct people per pain stops one loud voice from setting priorities. ✗ The sponsor's description of the work is enough to design the system. Shadowing finds steps nobody mentions; the description is a hypothesis. ✓ Discovery should end with a measurable problem statement the sponsor agrees to. Recap What to keep Name sponsor, users, owner and gatekeepers, and what each needs to say yes. Ask about the last real case, then watch the work. End with a problem statement that has a number and a baseline. Exercises Add a "severity" field to the notes (minor, blocks the claim) and change the ranking to weight blocking pains double. Does the order change? Write five discovery questions for the security team at Harbor Mutual. Rewrite the problem statement for a different sponsor goal: reducing claims leakage (overpayment) instead of time. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Say no early: score each use case on five tests, and only build the ones whose business case survives its weakest assumption. The problem Discovery produces more ideas than any team can build. Picking by excitement leads to the hardest, riskiest idea first. A simple, explicit score makes the choice arguable in a meeting, and an ROI model with a sensitivity check shows the sponsor what has to be true for the money to come back. Five fit tests Test Question 1 (poor) 5 (strong) Value How much does it move the sponsor's number? Nice to have Large, measured pain Feasibility Can current models do it reliably? Needs judgement models do badly Pattern the model already does well Data readiness Can we reach the inputs and the ground truth? No access, no labels Access granted, examples labelled Risk What does a mistake cost, and can a person catch it? Irreversible, unreviewed Reversible, reviewed Adoption Will the users want it? Threatens their role Removes work they hate Copy What you should see Copy Copy The floor matters more than the weights. "Auto-approve small claims" has the highest value but an irreversible, unreviewed risk; it goes on the roadmap for after trust is earned, not first. The ROI model Use the baseline from discovery and keep every assumption in one place so the sponsor can change it. Copy What you should see Copy Copy model_cost_per_claim is a placeholder: compute it from your own token counts and the current price list (lesson 31.15 does this properly). Which assumption breaks it? Copy What you should see Copy Copy Below about 3 minutes saved, or with adoption under a third, the case barely pays back in a year. That tells you what the pilot must prove: minutes saved per claim and real adoption, not model accuracy in isolation. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A use case with one very poor test (for example irreversible, unreviewed risk) should wait, whatever its total score. ✗ ROI should use the sponsor's estimate of time saved, since they know the business. It should use a measured baseline; the sponsor's estimate is an assumption to test. ✓ The sensitivity check tells you what the pilot has to prove. Recap What to keep Five tests, explicit weights, and a floor that blocks risky ideas. ROI from a measured baseline, with assumptions in one editable place. Find the assumption that breaks the case; make the pilot measure it. Exercises Add a sixth candidate from your own work and score it. Which test is hardest to score honestly? Add a one-off integration cost that only applies to the "Extract claim fields" use case and compare its payback with "Draft missing-document requests". The problem Automating a bad process produces a fast bad process. And the process in the operations manual is rarely the one people follow: handlers skip a step that never matters, add one the manual forgot, wait on a colleague for an hour. Time : about an hour. In plain words first The idea in one line Agree in writing what "done" means as numbers on a test set, what is not included, and how long it will take with the uncertainty shown. The problem "The AI should handle claims well" cannot be accepted or rejected. Without a measurable definition of done, the engagement ends in an argument, or never ends. The fix is old (a statement of work) with one change for AI systems: acceptance criteria are written as evals on an agreed test set. The scope document In scope (release 1): triage of claims emails into a draft claim; extraction of 14 named fields from email and PDF attachments; policy lookup (read-only); drafting of missing-document requests for handler approval; a review screen in the existing claims system. Out of scope: sending anything to customers without approval; photo damage assessment; payments; claims other than motor and home. Assumptions: read access to the policy API by week 2; 300 historical claims labelled by handlers by week 3; one pilot team of 8 handlers. Dependencies: security review slot in week 3; IT to add one field to the review screen. Acceptance criteria as evals Copy What you should see Copy Copy Extraction misses its target: the acceptance meeting now discusses which fields fail, not whether the system "feels good". Lesson 31.13 builds the eval suite behind these numbers. Estimating with the uncertainty visible A three-point estimate per task (optimistic, likely, pessimistic) gives an expected value and a spread. Summing variances, not worst cases, gives an honest buffer. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Commit to the 95% figure, and say which tasks carry the spread (here the review UI and security changes), so the customer can help remove it. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Acceptance criteria for an AI system should be numbers on an agreed test set. ✗ Out-of-scope items can be left unstated, since anything not listed is out. Unstated items become arguments; list the ones the customer is likely to assume. ✓ Summing task variances gives a smaller, more honest buffer than adding every worst case. Recap What to keep Scope = in, out, assumptions, dependencies. Acceptance criteria are evals with targets and a named test set. Estimate with three points; commit to a confidence level and show where the risk is. Exercises Add a criterion for the share of claims the system declines to process (sends to a human untouched). The readout One page, in this order: the decision asked for (for example, "move the pilot team to supervised and extend assisted to two more teams"); the result against the success criteria , with intervals; what went wrong and what changed because of it; cost per claim in production terms; risks and the plan for them ; what the next rung needs . Put the evidence in an appendix, not in the first page. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Each rung of the ladder has an explicit, measured entry test. ✗ If handlers like the tool, the pilot has succeeded. Liking matters for adoption, but the decision rests on the agreed metrics against the baseline. ✓ A baseline taken in different conditions (a storm week, a different claim mix) can make the pilot look better or worse than it is. Recap What to keep Shadow, assisted, supervised, then narrow autonomy; each rung earned. Compare with a like-for-like baseline and report intervals. The readout starts with the decision, not the method. Exercises Split the pilot data by claim type (motor, home) using a random label, and report each. What would you conclude if home showed no gain? Add a novelty check: compare the first two pilot weeks with the last two. What result would worry you? Draft the first five lines of the Harbor Mutual readout. Time : about 50 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line The FDE is the product team's eyes in the field: write down what customers needed and what you had to build, so the next deployment needs less of it. The problem Every deployment produces custom code. If it stays buried in one customer's repository, the next FDE builds it again. If everything is pushed into the product, the product fills with one customer's quirks. The skill is telling these apart and reporting it well. The field note A useful note has: the job the customer was trying to do , what got in the way (a missing feature, an awkward API, a gap in the docs), the workaround and how long it took, who else is likely to need it , and evidence (a trace, a metric, a quote). One paragraph each; no opinions without a case behind them. One-off or reusable? Copy What you should see Copy Copy The thresholds are a team agreement, not a law; the point is to decide with the same questions every time. Seeing patterns across deployments Copy What you should see Copy Copy Three of four deployments needed document parsing and approvals screens. That is a roadmap conversation, backed by counts rather than anecdotes. Tag notes with a small fixed vocabulary so counts like this mean something. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A field note needs evidence such as a trace, metric or quote. ✗ Anything a customer asks for twice should go into the product. Customer-specific logic belongs in their repo even if they ask often; generalise what many customers need. ✓ A fixed tag vocabulary makes patterns across deployments countable. Recap What to keep Job, obstacle, workaround, who else, evidence. Score one-off against reusable with the same questions each time. Tag notes so patterns across deployments can be counted. Time : four focused sessions of about an hour each, or four half-days if you build the stretch goals. In plain words first The idea in one line Do the job end to end on a fresh customer: discover, scope, build, prove, secure, roll out and hand over, then grade yourself against a fixed rubric. The brief Northwind Freight is a mid-sized logistics company. Its customer-service team of 22 people handles about 1,100 shipment-exception emails a day: delayed loads, damaged goods, wrong addresses, missing proof of delivery. Each email needs a case opened in the transport system with the shipment ID, exception type and urgency, and often a reply asking the customer for photos or a corrected address. The operations director (your sponsor) says: "We want AI to deal with these emails. Our best agents take 6 minutes each; new starters take 15. We lose key accounts when urgent cases sit for half a day." You have the sponsor for 30 minutes on day 1, and the team lead and two agents for an hour. Everything else is in the case pack below. Use the Harbor Mutual lessons as your method, not as your answer: the workflow, risks and numbers here differ. The case pack Copy What you should see Copy Copy The pack also states these constraints (treat them as interview findings): The transport system has a REST API with read access to shipments and a "create case" endpoint; there is no endpoint to change addresses or issue credits, and the IT lead wants it kept that way. Customer emails often include names, phone numbers and delivery addresses. The data protection officer must approve any new processor; the company already uses Claude through its cloud provider's approved region. Two agents keep a private spreadsheet of key-account contacts who "must be called, not emailed". Nobody else knows it exists. Urgent cases are supposed to be picked up within 2 hours; the team lead thinks the real median is about 5 hours on busy days. Day 1: discover and qualify Produce: a stakeholder map, the ranked pains, a one-paragraph problem statement with a measurable outcome, a fit score and an ROI range (lessons 31.4 and 31.5 ). Map today's workflow and mark the agent line ( 31.6 ). The private spreadsheet is a finding: decide what it means for the design. Day 2: scope and prototype Produce: the scope document with acceptance criteria as numbers on a test set ( 31.7 ); a golden set of at least 40 labelled cases drawn from the pack, with slices for exception type, key accounts and missing IDs ( 31.13 ); a working offline prototype of triage and extraction with validation and traces ( 31.8 ), using recorded outputs if you have no API key. Day 3: tools, trust and cost Produce: the tool manifest (read shipment, create case, propose reply) passing the agent-line check ( 31.9 , 31.14 ); the trust-boundary document with redaction; the eval report with per-slice scores, intervals and a release gate decision; the per-email cost model with a monthly range ( 31.15 ). Day 4: rollout and handover Produce: the trust-ladder plan with unlock metrics and a baseline plan ( 31.16 ); the adoption plan with champions and the telemetry you will watch ( 31.17 ); the readiness check, runbook and handover pack ( 31.18 ); one field note for the product team ( 31.19 ); and a 5-minute readout for the sponsor that starts with the decision you are asking for. The dossier and its check Copy What you should see Copy Copy The rubric Score each criterion 0 to 3: 0 missing, 1 present but unsupported, 2 supported by evidence, 3 supported and the trade-offs are explicit. Pass with 30 or more out of 42 and no criterion at 0. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The example scores above 30 and still misses the pass, only because the field note is absent, which is the point of the no-zero rule: a deployment that never reports back to the product has not finished the job. Add a fourth rung to the rollout plan (replies sent without approval for "pod_missing" emails only) and write the evidence you would need before the sponsor signs it. Any criterion at 0 means not yet, whatever the total. ✓ The dossier should let a reviewer check every claim against evidence.
